title: How to Lead Your Family When You Feel Like a Failure
excerpt: The qualification to lead your family was never your competence. It is your willingness to keep showing up, repenting, and pointing past yourself to God.
body:
Most parents, at some point, lie awake convinced they are failing their children. The temper they cannot fix. The patience they do not have. The faith they preach but do not feel. The sense that everyone else has this figured out and they alone are unfit for the people sleeping down the hall. If that is you, read this slowly. You are not disqualified. You may, in fact, be closer to the truth than the parents who feel sure of themselves.

The Bible is not a record of competent leaders. It is a record of God using broken ones who kept turning back to him.

## God has always led through failures

Look at who God put in charge. Abraham lied about his wife to save his own skin, twice. Jacob deceived his father and played favorites with his sons, and the damage rippled for generations. David, called a man after God's own heart, was a catastrophe of a father. Moses argued that he was the wrong man for the job and was right about most of his weaknesses. God led his people through every one of them.

The pattern is unmistakable, and it should loosen something in your chest. God does not wait for qualified parents because there are none. He uses the parent who keeps coming back to him over the parent who has it all together, because the second kind does not exist and the first kind is teachable. Your sense of inadequacy is not evidence you should quit. It may be the very thing that keeps you on your knees, which is exactly where a parent belongs.

## Repentance is the leadership

You will fail your children. The question is never whether, only what you do next. And here is the thing the competent-looking parents often miss: your repentance is not the interruption of your leadership. It is the leadership. When your children watch you fail, own it, turn back to God, and try again, they are learning the single most important thing you can teach them, which is what to do with their own failure.

A family does not need a flawless leader. It needs a leader who knows where to turn when they are not flawless. Lead from weakness, out loud. Let them see you ask God for help you clearly need. Paul learned that God's power is made perfect in weakness, and that he would rather boast in his weakness so that power could rest on him. That is not a consolation prize for failures. That is the actual mechanism. The cracked vessel is the one the light gets through.

## Show up tomorrow

Most of parenting is not won in great moments but in the refusal to quit after bad ones. You yelled tonight. You were absent this week. You said the wrong thing. None of that is final unless you let it become final by giving up. The single most powerful thing a struggling parent can do is show up again tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that.

Faithfulness over time covers a multitude of individual failures. The parent who is present and repentant across ten thousand ordinary days, most of them imperfect, is doing something a single spectacular failure cannot undo. Lamentations says God's mercies are new every morning. So is your chance to parent. You do not have to fix everything. You have to get up.

## Point past yourself

Here is the deepest relief, and the heart of it. You were never your children's savior. You cannot be, and the attempt to be is itself a kind of pride wearing the mask of love. There is already a Savior, and it is not you. Your job is not to be perfect for your children. It is to point them, with your imperfect life, to the One who is.

This frees you from a burden you were never meant to carry. You can stop pretending to be enough and start showing your children where real enough is found. The most honest thing you can say to your child is also the most freeing thing you can say to yourself: I get it wrong a lot, and there is Someone who never does, and we are both running to him together.

## This week

If you are carrying the weight of feeling like a failure, do two things this week. First, repent out loud where your children can see it, not as a show but as the lesson it actually is, so they learn what to do with their own failures by watching you handle yours. Second, get up tomorrow and show up again, imperfect, undeterred, present. You do not have to save your children. You only have to keep pointing them to the One who can, and keep walking that road yourself, one ordinary day at a time.
